raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? 
    I notice that when the pandemic happened in 2020, a lot of things in the U.S. changed. Many people died, a lot lost their jobs, and people started spending more money on food from stores instead of eating at restaurants. I also see that people didn’t hang out as much, and even after the pandemic, things never really went back to normal. 
    2. What do you wonder?
    I wonder how long these changes will last and if people’s habits will ever completely go back to normal. For example, will people keep working from home, shopping online more, and hanging out less? I also wonder how these long-term lifestyle changes will affect young people like me in the future. 
    3. How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to my community because the pandemic also changed the way people around me live and work. Many people in Japan started wearing masks and spending less time outside or meeting friends. Schools and workplaces moved to online systems, and habits like wearing masks all the time still remain. 
    4. Create a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
    “How Covid Ruined Americans’ Everyday Life and It Still Hasn’t Gone Back.”

1. What do you notice?
    
    Almost all the graphs spiked during the 2020 Covid pandemic, except for third through eighth grade U.S levels, eating at restaurants, and time socializing with others. Most increases were a straight jump up, meaning a sharp exponential graph.
    
    
    2. What do you wonder?

1. I notice that in each of the graphs, there is a sudden increase or decrease during the time period of COVID-19. For example, the Unemployment claims graph went from fewer than half a million claims before March 2020 to over 6 million unemployment claims around March 
    2. I wonder at what point each graph starts to even out and go back to its track before COVID. Many of the graphs seem to look similar to before the pandemic, and I wonder if it was because of the pandemic ending or the improvement of the U.S..
    3. This has made an impact on me and my community because we have seen a shift between before the pandemic, during, and after. During the pandemic, the employment rates were high, our test scores were going down, we spent less time socializing, and more. Now that COVID is not as big of a problem anymore, everything is switching back to relatively how it was before the pandemic. Some changes are not completely back to normal, such as test scores and time socializing, but we are back on the track we were originally supposed to be. 
    4. "A ripple in time"

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
    
    The graph shows a dramatic spike in web searches for “How to cut your own hair” in March 2020, aligning with the start of the COVID-19 pandemic and lockdowns. Prior to this point, search interest remained consistently low. After peaking, the trend declined sharply but stayed somewhat elevated compared to pre-pandemic levels, suggesting a lasting, though reduced, interest in DIY grooming.
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    
    I wonder how long people continued cutting their own hair after salons reopened, and whether some individuals permanently changed their habits as a result. It also raises curiosity about whether similar search spikes occurred for other self-care routines during the pandemic, and how that reflects changes in consumer behavior and independence.
    
    3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
    
    This graph is a clear reflection of how communities quickly adapted to sudden disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic. With salons closed, people turned to the internet to find ways to manage basic grooming needs themselves. In my community, this led to a surge in shared tips, YouTube tutorials, and even virtual haircutting lessons—fostering both resourcefulness and a temporary shift away from professional services.
    
    4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    
    "Pandemic Hair Panic: How Lockdowns Sparked a DIY Haircut Surge"

raw_comment:
Covid social(media?)lizing 
    
    
    The graph clearly shows a significant jump in socializing in 2021, likely driven by the easing of pandemic restrictions and a strong desire for reconnection after prolonged isolation. However, this surge was followed by a decrease in 2022. This decline could be attributed to lingering COVID-19 concerns, the emergence of new variants, or the persistence of social habits formed during the pandemic.
    
    My main question revolves around the definition of "socializing" used in the graph. The term is broad, encompassing everything from in-person interactions at school or social events to online communication via social media. The lack of specificity makes it difficult to fully understand the data. Clarification on the types of socializing included would greatly improve the graph's interpretability
    
    Like many communities, we've seen a growing reliance on social media for communication, sometimes at the expense of in-person interactions. The graph, even without specifying the type of socializing, highlights the pandemic's impact on our social lives and the importance of finding a healthy balance between online and offline connections. It makes me consider how I can engage meaningful relationships in a world increasingly mediated by technology

    What do you notice?
    I noticed people spending more money on groceries than going out to eat at restaurants
    and how more people did online shopping and how reading and math scores dropped a
    lot in the US and spending time socializing and talking dropped.

    What do you wonder?
    I wonder if people will ever go back to going out more in their community and possibly
    doing more out to eat and shopping and socializing much more.
    ●
    How does this relate to you and your community?

    to stay home for the rest of the year and having to talk to all my friends online and learn
    online.
    ●
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    Life after COVID

The first thing I notice when looking at the graphs is that during March of 2020, when the pandemic started, all of the graphs had a drastic change. For instance, the total number of deaths, unemployment claims, used car prices, and at home tutorials all spiked.

    "The Affects of Covid Continue"

raw_comment: Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  " “Adapting to Change: How COVID Reshaped Our Daily Life” by Camrynn of Barnstable High School, Mass.; "Pandemic Impact: Is the U.S. Truly Back On Its Feet After Such Harsh Years?" by Amina of Southwest High School, Minneapolis, Minn.; two headlines from Academy of Saint Elizabeth, Convent Station, N.J. -- “Lockdown Life: How Has It Changed the Country?” by Juliana and “The Covid Curveball:  The Pandemic That Changed Everything” by Giulia;  three headlines from Perth Amboy High School, N.J. -- "Life, Disrupted: A Pandemic Snapshot" by Melanny, “A Silent Aftermath: How COVID-19 Changed the Way We Learn, Spend, and Connect” by Lavon and “Life in the Time of COVID: The Transformative Impact on American Daily Life!” by Esmeily and two headlines from Langley High School, McLean, Va. -- “Unmasked Trends: How a Virus Redefined the Everyday” by Lekha and “The Pandemic Has Passed, but Effects Still Linger” by Lila.

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed about this graph was that some trends were already underway before the pandemic. Deaths, online shopping, women in the workforce, “how to cut your own hair” searches, and spending on groceries were all on the rise. Also, education scores and time socializing with others were both declining. These trends suggest that the pandemic only exacerbated existing issues in the country. I also noticed that many changes during the pandemic have not returned to their pre-pandemic levels. This suggests that the pandemic has caused disruptions to the country that will persist for a while. I wonder if there were any positive outcomes from the pandemic. All nine graphs depict technically negative trends; does that mean there were no positive outcomes of the pandemic? I also wonder if any of these lasting impressions of the pandemic will correct themselves over time, like others have. This relates to me and my community because, as an American who experienced the pandemic first-hand, I have witnessed the changes in the country.
    
    Headline: Did COVID-19 make an irreversible impact on the United States?

## 1. Chart type
A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |

raw_comment:
The graph demonstrates changes that the pandemic made to the everyday lives of American citizens in terms of deaths, unemployment, prices, etc.  I initially noticed the graph illustrating money spent on food and how it shows the money that people spent on groceries and in restaurants.  I noticed that the March 2020 rates went up for groceries and down for restaurants, as I expected.  The amount of money that people spent on restaurants has increased since 2020, and has surpassed money spent on groceries as of 2023.  I also noticed that time socializing with others decreased after 2020, but was also on a downward slope before the pandemic hit.  The most drastic changed seemed to be the ‘How to cut your own hair’ web searches, which skyrocketed after the pandemic.  I wonder if this web search stemmed from social media trends because I remember seeing haircut tutorials on my social media during the COVID pandemic.  I also wonder why the share of men in the labor force was not a displayed graph, and if this was because the share of women in the labor force was the only notable change.  This affects me and my community because my family stopped going to restaurants during the pandemic and definitely spent more on groceries as well as online shopped more than shopping in person.  
    Headline: COVID 19: 5 Years Before vs. 5 Years After

raw_comment:
In these graphs, I noticed that the only areas that experienced a downwards trend were U.S. scores and socialization. Other than those, all of the other graphs experienced an increase in the studied area. I also observed that pre-pandemic people spent more money on groceries than restaurants. However, now people spend more on restaurants. I am curious whether this money is being spent in person at restaurants or through online platforms like Uber Eats. I wonder this because of the increase that the graph depicted about online shopping. I am also curious as to whether this increase in online shopping/spending has hindered or helped our economy. Finally, I wonder how the U.S. scores might change after President Trumps executive orders regarding the department of education. This topic impacts me because having lived through covid and now post covid, I am actively contributing to areas like an increase in online shopping and I am impacted by lower education scores. 
    
    Title: Going up?: The U.S. after The COVID-19 Pandemic

raw_comment:
Headline: Changes in 2020: Covid-19 Impacts on the U.S. people
    The graph shows that in 2020, there were significant changes in various aspects of Americans' lives. In terms of unemployment claims, they shot up immensely in 2020. The same goes for total deaths, used car prices, and 'how to cut your hair' searches. I also noticed that many metrics returned to their "average" pre-COVID-19 levels. However, some trends seem to persist indefinitely. For instance, the declining U.S. score (3rd grade through 8th) remained downward until today. However, it is difficult to say if COVID-19 caused these changes in online shopping and U.S. scores because they were already on an upward/downward trend before COVID-19. I, therefore, wonder if the impacts of COVID-19 (post 2020) on these aspects of the U.S. people's lives are as impactful as they first seem and how these aspects may have interacted with each other. For instance, do unemployment claims correlate with the prices of used cars and, furthermore, the prices/economic state of the country? I believe this graph encourages readers to examine the interplay between various aspects and to consider the broader impact of COVID-19 on these factors. This relates to me and my community because I lived through the Covid-19 pandemic. I am able to relate to several of these aspects. COVID-19 had a significant impact on me, and as a result, I can attest to the correlation between these aspects and COVID-19.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that there is a total of 9 graphs, all showing how the pandemic affected life. The first shows an increase in death rates after March 2020, a direct effect of the possibly fatal disease. Unemployed claims spiked from below 2 million to 6 million claims a week, likely caused by businesses shutting down. In previous years, the amount of women in the workforce has increased but declined during the pandemic. I assume that many moms were forced to stay home with their children because they attended online school. During COVID, people spent more money on groceries than restaurants. The stark, 40% increase in used car prices shows how large an issue inflation is. Online shopping also increased during the pandemic. Socialization fell drastically in 2020 and has not recovered, showing the change in culture after COVID-19. Students from 3rd to 8th grade went from being 0.2 years ahead to being more than 0.4 years behind in grades. The final graph shows the spike in people searching  “How to cut your own hair” in 2020. This is evidently due to social distancing.
    2. I wonder how post-pandemic statistics compare to 2000. What about the pandemic caused inflation to rise? What steps did it take to recover from the negative impact of COVID-19?
    3. This relates to me because my life was greatly affected by the pandemic. The way I learned and how my parents work have changed. The spike in prices affects the cost of living of my family and me. 
    4. The Price of a Pandemic”

raw_comment:
I noticed that this graph depicts changes the U.S has gone through since the COVID Pandemic. The most noticeable differences include constant spikes in death rates. Other rate changes include the money spend on groceries, unemployment claims, used car prices, and the google searches for "How to cut your own hair". Socializing time has dropped as well, and has not returned from what it used to be pre- March 2020. The drop in test scores is the most worrying. 
    I wonder why the rates of socializing has not gone back up more. I would think people would jump at the chance to see each other. I guess they were still worried about getting sick, or maybe people have isolated themselves so much they live their lives through a screen. 
    This graph relates to me and my community because the whole world was affected by the pandemic. These graphs are probably the most relatable I have yet to see. 
    Headline: 2020 to 2025 - How Life has Changed

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I noticed people spending more money on groceries than going out to eat at restaurants and how more people did online shopping and how reading and math scores dropped a lot in the US and spending time socializing and talking dropped. 
    What do you wonder? 
    I wonder if people will ever go back to going out more in their community and possibly doing more out to eat and shopping and socializing much more. 
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This is related to my community because COVID affects me going to school, me having to stay home for the rest of the year and having to talk to all my friends online and learn online.
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    Life after COVID

What do you notice?
    
    More people during Covid spent money on groceries rather than spending money on restaurants. 
    
    
    • What do you wonder?

raw_comment:
It’s fascinating to see how fluctuant post-pandemic recovery has been across different vectors of American life. For example, used car prices continue to rise instead of returning to pre-COVID levels which alludes to supply chain disruptions which continue impacting today’s world or shifts in consumer behavior. Meanwhile, weekly death rates in the U.S. remain significantly higher than before the pandemic which could a direct result of the health complications and aggressive flue seasons, however, it could also have been a social issue formed during the pandemic regarding vaccine skepticism and health care becoming a social cleavage. 
    
    On the other hand, some areas like unemployment claims appear to have stabilized, reflecting a return to normalcy in parts of the economy.
    
    One question comes to mind when analyzing lingering effects of the pandemic which is if we are still actively experiencing trends which have not correct themselves years later, can we truly say we are in a “post-pandemic” era, or is this shift a stagnant new normal.

raw_comment:
Pandemic’s Fluctuating Pulse: How COVID’s Fever Charts Told America’s Story  
    I notice that some trends started before the pandemic, and some were more dependent on the pandemic. Such as online shopping, U.S scores, and time spent with others. However, some seem to be completely dependent on the pandemic, such as ‘How To Cut Your Own Hair Searches’ and 'Unemployment Rates’ which can be attributed to the economy’s state at the time, and the increase of time spent on the internet. I wonder what factors played a part in these roles. For example, does online interaction count as socialization, as social networks, such as TikTok, peaked interest during the pandemic. Additionally, what demographics are being polled? For the online shopping, it relates to the community, as a lack of teachers is still surging our country. As a student, I have noticed post-pandemic the lack of subs who care, and strong new hires within schools. Considering my community is very close to the D.C suburbs, women employment is a very important aspect of D.C life. The nation’s capital, where the U.S is represented to the global stage, we should have an accurate image of our country and the perspectives within it. The pandemic helped shape a more adequate share of women in the workforce, which could be due to epiphanies about interests, or more time to start their own business and for entrepreneurship in general. This goes back to my original question of what factors played a role in this graph’s increase.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I've noticed from the used car prices graph on how drastically it has increased despite unemployment rates being at an all time high from only 2 years ago. Of course with time, people began to regain their jobs, but buying a car is a large purchase that is necessary for the layout of many US states/cities. People depend on transportation, so it's interesting how there has been a 40% increase when people may not have fully gotten back on their economic paths.
    
    What do you wonder?
    How does the increase in online shopping affect our planet? Many  fast fashion shops, like SHEIN, have boomed in sales with the quarantine and have seen a steady rise, but all the excesses clothes must go somewhere. Trends come and go, people ultimately throw away hundreds of clothes that will impact our environment severely. While online shopping allows for widespread access and no longer requires one to physically leave their house to shop, this quick accessibility can cause a multitude of problems from the packaging to the clothing itself. 
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    Both graphs impact my close community and I, as I will soon be buying my own things, such as the cars and clothes mentioned. It's good to put into perspective how things have changed, so I can plan my future in a (hopefully) more affordable way. 
    
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea?
    What were the Booms and Dooms of the quarantine?

raw_comment: The graphs show how various aspects of Americans' lives before, during, & after the pandemic, including aspects that I wouldn't normally think about. What's interesting to notice is certain trends that began before the pandemic that are often attributed entirely to the pandemic. For instance, time socializing with others was already on a steep decline from ~2019, U.S. scores already had a steady downward trend, & online shopping was already on the rise. I wonder if the increase in used car prices is because of the new demand for used cars, allowing for retailers to hike up prices. What are the contributors for the decline in US scores beginning in ~2017?

raw_comment:
Used car prices rose dramatically, peaking in February 2022 which I don't fully understand. If people aren't driving then why are car prices so high? Is it because of the scarcity of microchips?
    Online shopping increased rapidly and still remains above the pre-pandemic trend. The how to cut your own hair spike was a funny addition. Students' academic performance fell behind in both math and reading. Some questions I had were, will some of these changes become permanent, like online shopping and remote socializing? How long will it take for academic scores to recover to pre-pandemic levels, and how is this influenced by AI and a lack of actual learning? Why have used car prices stayed relatively high compared to pre-pandemic levels? This relates directly to my community—during the pandemic, schools shut down, grocery stores were often crowded while restaurants were nearly empty, and everyone suddenly became more dependent on online shopping and remote interactions. Many people lost jobs or worked from home. Students I know still feel the academic impact, and some families continue to balance childcare and work in new ways.

raw_comment: Going from left to right, up to down, the graphs illustrate the following impacts of the stay-at-home orders: 1. While not directly related to the stay-at-home orders, the orders reflect the severity of the pandemic as more and more people become infected as the pandemic spreads 2. Millions of people are laid off due to the digital incompatibility of many jobs (i.e. people that are unable to work enclosed inside their homes) 3. The majority of women decide to tend to their infant children post-orders due to propensities caused by proximity and quit working initially, however because of the higher mortality rate of men, the net amount of women in the labor force decreases at a slower rate of men dying from COVID at higher rates, causing the share of women in the labor force to increase 4. Restaurants close due to social distancing so the alternative is groceries 5. Used car prices increase due to an independent factor unrelated to the COVID pandemic, the car prices should decrease as demand for transportation decreases because of the stay-at-home orders, so it is due to an unrelated factor 6. Online shopping increases due to social distancing 7. People become socially isolated because of staying at home 8. Online learning is substantially less effective than in-person learning 9. Barber shops close due to social distancing

raw_comment:
Each of the nine graphs show how life in the US changed in some manner during the pandemic, before and after COVID-19. The first thing that I noted was the incredible spike in deaths starting around March 2020, and the spike tied to the start of the pandemic. The other major change was the incredible spike in initial unemployment claims, almost 6 million a week above anything before COVID-19.
    
    Another change was how people were spending their money. Grocery spending increased while restaurant spending dipped lower than the pre-pandemic level. I also found it interesting that the spikes in used car prices and the online shopping levels were both also above pre-pandemic trends. For parents, perhaps the most alarming trend is the downward trend in test scores for students, especially in math, which could potentially affect a generation.
    
    This connected to my own experience because I remember the school closures, the shift from in person to online, and how everyone had to adapt. All of this change in lifestyle affected academic, social, and emotional education. It also reduced times spent socializing, which reminds me of how isolated I had felt during the time.
    
    Headline: How COVID-19 Changed Everything From Learning To Living

raw_comment:
What do you notice?  
    The graph I am interested in shows math and reading scores in 3rd to 8th graders. I notice that from 2019 to 2022 there is a big decline in both areas. And from 2022 to 2023, the scores begin to rise again, with math scores rising at a faster rate.
    
    What do you wonder?  
    Before 2019, the graph indicates that math scores served as a baseline, while reading scores started 0.2 years ahead. I wonder why math and reading scores aligned at the 2019 baseline. Additionally, I am curious about how these trends will affect the future workforce.
    How does this relate to you and your community? 
    I was in my last year of middle school in 2020 when COVID-19 struck. I experienced the decline firsthand and felt discouraged to continue working hard in math and reading for the next couple of years.
    
    Catchy headline: Covid strike

raw_comment:
After looking at the graph, I noticed that it contains 9 graphs that compare how the pandemic has changed the lives of Americans. The data in these graphs was recorded in the five years before and after the lockdown orders that began in March of 2020. The topics analyzed in the nine graphs are total U.S. deaths, unemployment claims, share of women in the labor force, money spent on food, used car prices, online shopping, time socializing with others, U.S. scores, and “how to cut your own hair” web searches. During lockdown, unemployment claims spiked drastically and increased to almost six million claims per week. Online shopping increased during the pandemic and returned to the pre-pandemic trend after lockdown ended. The U.S. test scores of children between third and eighth grade have decreased since before the pandemic. 
    After looking at the graph, I wonder why the amount of time people spend socializing with others is so low. Also, I wonder why used car prices increased between 2020 and 2022. In 2024, why did people spend more money on food from restaurants than on groceries? How would this data differ if the pandemic had never happened? 
    This graph relates to my community as it displays the changes in my life as a result of the pandemic. Very few of the topics compared in the graphs have the same numbers recorded before and after the pandemic.
    A headline for this graph is “Changes in the lives of U.S. Citizens”.

raw_comment:
Headline: The pandemic has passed, but effects still linger
    
    Overall, although the effects of the pandemic were greatest during 2020-2021, Americans still experience the impacts of the pandemic today. As a student in high school, I've noticed the declining trend in the time socializing with others as a major impact from the pandemic. Since returning from online school, students are increasingly less likely to interact with one another, especially as many students decide to turn to their phones in their free time as opposed to starting a conversation with others they're physically sitting around. Additionally, although the US scores on reading and math exams are only for 3rd-8th graders, my current high school teachers have mentioned the trend is also present in high school, especially evident in the grading of nationwide exams like AP exams that have begun making their rubrics slightly easier for students. The time online definitely set students back, and the education system is having to create new standards for students to adjust to their learning setbacks. I do wonder about the used car prices graph because there was an extremely steep incline all the way up to February 2022. Although prices have begun decreasing in recent years, I'm still confused as to why the prices shot up this much for used cars.

raw_comment:
I noticed the pandemic had a sharp spike in several indicators  during March 2020. US deaths skyrocketed, yet later returned to pre-pandemic levels. Additionally, shifted spending from restaurants to groceries, and led to a long-term rise in online shopping. Students test scores dropped, social interaction decreased, and several women temporarily left the labor force in large numbers. 
    
    I wonder if students ever recover from learning loss and whether online shopping and reduced socialization are permanent changes. I am also curious how the workforce will continue to adapt, specifically for women and children. 
    
    School became harder during and after the pandemic, as many are catching up from being academically behind. My community shops online more, and socialize differently - less frequently and more cautious. 
    
    Headline: Unmasked Trends: How a Virus Redefined the Everyday

raw_comment:
Headline - "The Profound Implications of COVID-19 on our Society"
    There are nine graphs in total, all displaying trends before and after COVID-19 within American society. As shown, there has been an attempt to return to normalcy as indicated by the trend lines after COVID-19 being gradually restored to what they previously were. Two graphs in particular stick out to me: "Time socializing with others" and "U.S. scores, 3rd through 8th." I wonder that due to the fact that socializing stimulates brain development, if that a decrease in scores is more due to social deprivation than the halt in learning when schools shut down. As a current junior in high school, I have noticed some changes within my community. Namely, that socialization has decreased among my peers from what it once was, from-what I believe to be-a hangover from social distancing.

raw_comment: It is fascinating to see the educational scores graphs' immense decline. Though many point to COVID-19 as the catalyst for poorer reading and math scores, the graph shows that scores have been steadily declining before the height of the pandemic. What is the reason for this early decline? Yes, COVID-19 exacerbated poor educational habits, but it is interesting to see how scores, math specifically, have already been on a decline since 2017. It is also interesting to see how far math scores have declined since COVID-19, leaving students almost 0.6 years behind in scores in 2022. On the other hand, reading scores have declined but not as drastically as math.

raw_comment: Of the nine graphs presented, all of them show notable changes in different trends as the COVID 19 pandemic hit. Of these graphs, I find the "'how to cut your own hair' web trends" to give comic relief to the depressing nature of some of the graphs, such as "Total U.S. deaths" and "Time socializing with others". Regarding the Total U.S. deaths chart, there is certainly a change in deaths, likely as a result of COVID. Looking at the averages of the chart, it seems that as a country, the United States has returned to its pre-COVID rates. I find this relieving, as it shows that that COVID truly is a thing of the past. Looking at some of these other graphs, it seems like we haven't totally recovered from COVID, though I believe that this may be to other factors such as changes in government, recessions, wars, ect. Overall, the data of these graphs shocks me, as I did not realize just how stark the changes of the pandemic were, but the data makes sense.

For one, used car prices have not returned back to pre-pandemic prices and instead are continuing to trend upward. raw_comment: I notice that these graphs show the incline or decline of certain aspects/activities in life before and after covid occurred. I notice that the unemployment claims significantly increased in March 2020, going from a little more than 0 a week to 6 million claims per week. I also noticed that the used car prices was very low (below 10%) before covid, and now has continued to increase, especially when 2021 hit. The used car prices has not returned to the pre-pandemic price levels since. I wonder why the socializing time level is still really low, even after covid ended. Before the pandemic, the levels were high, then dropped during covid, and now are still at a low. I also wonder what the reason is for the clear pattern in total US deaths, it seems to go high to low continuously in a pattern. I wonder what the main cause of these deaths are. This relates to me and my community because I lived through covid, and I experienced many of these aspects in my life that I did less of once covid started. For example, I couldn't see people/socialize as much and I didn't go out to restaurants as much during the pandemic. I noticed that my experiences through the pandemic for these two aspects align/match the graphs findings. Headline: How did the pandemic change our lives: Pandemic rates still effecting us today

raw_comment:
Headline: “Life After Lockdown: How Our Community Evolved—and What’s Next”
    
    The graphs compare key indicators before, during, and after the pandemic and reveal significant shifts across economic, social, and educational dimensions: death rates fluctuated sharply; unemployment claims spiked at the onset before settling at low levels; restaurant spending fell while grocery expenditures rose, only for dining out to later surpass grocery bills; used‑car prices climbed to a peak in February 2022; women’s labor‑force participation dipped and then recovered by 2022; online shopping remained elevated as a continuing trend; social interactions declined markedly compared to pre‑2020; student test scores in grades 3–8 fell from 2019 baselines—particularly in math—while reading proved more resilient; and searches for “how to cut your own hair” surged in 2022 before leveling off. These patterns underscore the pandemic’s broad and lasting impact on daily life.I wonder if student performance will bounce back to where it was before the pandemic, especially in math, and what steps will help them catch up. This relates to my community because we all went through these changes. Personally, my family still buys more groceries than we eat out at restaurants out of habit of the pandemic.

## 1. Chart type
A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |
raw_comment:

I first noticed that the death rate increased around 2020 which is due to covid. I wonder why the test scores decreased so rapidly after the pandemic hit and I wonder how this will affect the future of learning for the children who were in 3rd to 8th grade. This relates to my community because I lived through COVID-19 and had to be completely isolated from school, friends, and life when the pandemic hit. 
    Headline: Covid-19: The Effect the Pandemic Had on Society

raw_comment:
Headline- "Five Years Later: How the Pandemic Still Affects Us"
    
    The graphs depict how key aspects of life in the U.S. changed before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. One thing I noticed is that the total of U.S. deaths spiked multiple times after March 2020, way above the 2015-19 average. I also noticed that socializing time dropped in 2020, however, it still hasn’t returned to pre-pandemic levels. I wonder why the socializing level is still low and hasn't bounced back yet, even though restrictions have eased. Also, I wonder how the changes in social habits might affect long-term mental health and our community bonds. This relates to me and my community because, due to the pandemic, many students like me have experienced learning loss, which is reflected in the math and reading scores. Also, my family still usually orders groceries and most things online, even after restrictions have been lowered.

raw_comment:
These nine graphs display how the United States has changed since the COVID-19 pandemic. Americans were ordered to quarantine and every aspect of life was affected. I noticed that when COVID hit, unemployment claims reached around 6 million claims per week and death tolls reached around 80,000 per week. This affected the emotional and employment stability of millions of Americans. Along with this, the prices on food and cars increased causing many Americans to fall into poverty. Something that is very concerning for Americans is that time spent socializing with others and test scores in both reading and math have been decreasing since the pandemic hit. I wonder how this will affect the future of public school education. This affects my community because people are still facing the effects of job instability and inflation from the pandemic.
    Headline: COVID Aftershocks

A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |

## 1. Chart type
A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |

raw_comment: I notice that there was a dramatic spike in U.S. deaths as well as unemployment claims beginning in March 2020. I also noticed a shift in consumer behavior, for example, people spending more money on groceries and less on restaurants, as well as a dramatic rise in online shopping. I also noticed that U.S. test scores in both reading and math, and time spent socializing, largely dropped. I wonder how long it will take for these test scores to go back to how they were before the pandemic, or if they ever will. I also wonder why some shifts, like online shopping, stayed in a rising trend, while other shifts, such as people buying groceries, reverted to the way they were after the original spike. This relates to me and my community because it illustrates the lasting effects of the pandemic on my life. A headline for this graph could be, "Effects of the Pandemic: Beneficial or Not?".

## 1. Chart type
A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |

raw_comment:
Headline- The COVID Curveball: The Pandemic That Changed Everything
    
    What do you notice?
    In these graphs, I notice major shifts beginning in March 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic started. Unemployment claims spiked dramatically, while time spent socializing dropped. People began spending more on groceries and less at restaurants. Academic scores (especially in math) fell, likely because students had a harder time focusing during remote learning. Used car prices dipped in 2020 but then skyrocketed after 2021. Altogether, the graphs clearly show how the pandemic dramatically changed daily life for Americans
    
    What do you wonder? 
    What made some trends temporary (like haircut searches) and others more permanent (like online shopping)? How long will it take for student learning levels to fully recover, especially in math? It's been 5 years since COVID, and they still aren't near where they were pre-pandemic. Will car prices or grocery spending ever return to their pre-pandemic trends?
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This graph relates to my community because I experienced the pandemic and the changes it made to my life. As related to the graph, I socialized less with my friends, and as a result of online school, I felt like I learned much less. My parents, while still employed, shopped online much more and only ordered online groceries. They saw the changes in prices as well.

## 1. Chart type
A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

|---|---|---|

| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I notice this graph is showing the difference from pre-pandemic to the pandemic in issues in the US. I notice issues of prices and money spent went drastically up. The pandemic caused a spike in the prices, and  things like unemployment rates to go up. Graphs that went down were to do with education, and socialization showing how the pandemic changed the world. 
    What do you wonder?

raw_comment: In this graph I noticed that all the data being looked at increased, except for the activities that involved socialization, like time with others and U.S. test scores in elementary and middle school. Society still has not gotten back to where we were pre pandemic. The things that decreased have started to slowly increase, but the things that increased during the pandemic, rapdily decreased. I wonder if society will ever get back to where we were before the pandemic. I also wonder if test scores will start to plateau or if the education system will regain the scores. This relates to my community because I am affected by all of these categories, and I never even realized some of them at changed so drastically. I would title this graph: Covid Consequences, Life After Lockdown

This relates to me and my community because it shows how the pandemic and lockdown have negatively impacted those around me, the economy, and the country currently. raw_comment:
Observations - In the years leading up to March 2020 (2015-19), the total US deaths per week were numbering below 60,000, with the spike in 2018 being the sole exception. Unemployment claims were also relatively low, but they skyrocketed in March 2020 at 6 million claims per week. The share of women in the workforce decreased, but gradually increased beyond its pre pandemic numbers. Online shopping saw a sharp increase after March 2020, and so did the price of used cars. People began socializing a lot less, (possibly as a byproduct of social distancing, as also seen with the increased web searches of “How to Cut Your Own Hair”) and US Scores 3rd grade thru 8th declined. 
    
    Questions - Beyond the initial shock, how has the pandemic changed daily life in the U.S? What long-term effects are we seeing (or will see) in education, the economy, and social behaviors? And most importantly, how do we measure recovery - by numbers or by well-being?
    
    Relation to Community - These trends hit close to home in NJ. Most, if not all communities have faced an unemployment crisis and education gaps. These effects can still be felt up to this day. 
    
    Headline - Ctrl + Alt + COVID: Unpacking the Metrics Behind America’s Pause!

raw_comment:
What do you notice?  
    The graph I am particularly interested in shows math and reading scores from 3rd to 8th grade. I notice that from 2019 to 2022, there is a steep decline in both areas. However, from 2022 to 2023, the scores begin to improve, with math scores rising at a faster rate.
    
    What do you wonder?  
    Before 2019, the graph indicates that math scores served as a baseline, while reading scores started 0.2 years ahead. In 2019, the scores converged before the expected decline that followed. I wonder why math and reading scores aligned at the 2019 baseline. Additionally, I am curious about how these trends will affect the future workforce, especially as students who struggled after 2020 enter it.
    
    How does this relate to you and your community? 
    I was in my last year of elementary school in 2020 when COVID-19 struck. I experienced the decline firsthand and felt discouraged to continue working hard in math and reading for the next couple of years. I also saw my peers feeling similarly.
    
    Catchy headline: How COVID-19 Impacts Our Past, Present, and Future

raw_comment:
Notice:
    I noticed how the US economy changed once COVID hit, and we have recovered in some parts better than others. For example, the share of women in the labor force has had its ups and downs, but has slowly increased from what it was pre-pandemic. I notice that all of these statistics were affected super harshly by the pandemic.  I notice that “Unemployment claims” and “‘How to cut your own hair’” graphs are nearly identical.
     
    Wonder:
    I wonder if any aspects of our country were changed for the better. Did COVID help smaller communities in ways that aren't shown in these graphs, which only show negative impact? I wonder how many people were put out of a job because of the pandemic. How did they get some of these statistics?
    
    Relation to my community:
    This relates to our community because COVID affected all of us when we had to do online learning. It also affected how we socialized with others and set back many younger kids, like my sister, in developing social skills and emotional awareness. I remember doing homework by myself a lot more and having to learn how to use my resources to figure things out that I couldn't comprehend. The pandemic also helped me get a hold of my friends and talk with them without having to see them face to face, because that is how we had to do it during quarantine.
    
    Catchy Headline: "COVID-19 and the impactful effects it had on America"

raw_comment:
I notice that there is a predictable trend in each graph shown, spanning across several different parts of our lives. Each graph shown had a clearly dramatic disruption as covid hit. I notice how much everyday lives were changed during that time and most of which in a negative way. I also notice that in several of the graphs that the trend from the pre-pandemic time seemed to continue where it left off towards the end of the pandemic, which is a good sign. However, some of the graphs don’t resume where they left off and change directions in some way. 
    
    Over time, will the trends from before the pandemic come back? Will used car prices and U.S. deaths decrease to what they were before? Will socialization increase over time? There are several different graphs, and not all have rebounded since covid so it leaves us with the question if these things will return to “normal.” 
     
    This relates to my community, as well as most of the world around me because Covid entirely changed the lives of everyone. It changed school, we didn’t go back after spring break then we had hybrid and zoom. It changed the social aspect and how we communicate now could be a reflection of that. The world was not very connected during that time which is a reflection on why the social interaction graph still hasn’t rebounded to where it was before the pandemic. Though the pandemic is over, the lasting effects of it are not, and many of these things may never go back to how they were before.

raw_comment:
What I noticed: I noticed that many graphs were already either on a relatively steady increase or decrease, but most had a spike either in the positive or negative direction during the peak of the pandemic in 2020. One graph where I noticed this a lot was in the online shopping graph, where the graph was going at a pretty steady incline, but then in 2020, there was a big spike in people online shopping more.
    What I wonder: I wonder why a lot of the graphs are pretty contradictory to what you would assume they would look like, such as the graph displaying social time with others. This graph obviously plummeted during the pandemic, but then after the pandemic was done, it was still very low, even though I thought more people wanted to socialize with others because they hadn't for so long.
    How it relates to my community: It relates to my community because a lot of these graphs were very true and similar to how my community was during the pandemic, such as the graph displaying used car prices. When my family needed a new car after the pandemic, we were going to get a used car, but the prices were so high, we just decided to get a new car because the price gap was not that much, and the gap in wuality was quite substantial.
    Catchy Headline: "How Covid-19 changed lives nationwide."

I noticed that all graphs drastically changed in March of 2020, as this was when COVID was starting to become a worldwide emergency. Most of these graphs reflected a negative trend because of what people were experiencing at the time.

    I remember online learning and social distancing, I remember all of the challenges and things that everyone had to overcome during this time period.
    I'd title these graphs "How COVID-19 affected trends in the US"

## 1. Chart type
A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that for all the graphs, when it was good to have higher data, then it was lower after 2020. When it was better to be lower, it was higher after 2020. This showed me that the pandemic really affected human life in many ways. I also noticed that in general, after the pandemic began, data was more inconsistent. Naturally, data isn't always exactly gradual but in these graphs the data stays generally consistent. However, after COVID hit, things changed a lot from the original information but continued to change abruptly even after that. 
    2) I wonder how people who make these graphs can determine the information to put as data. Like, how do people know how many people are partaking in a survey or how calculating with averages, etc, can change how the graph looks? I just wonder how the whole process of creating graphs based on real life stays accurate. 
    3) This relates to me and my community because every focus for these graphs represents something that either directly happened to someone, or occurred around them that they saw. For me personally, I certainly noticed the used car prices when my family had to get a car, and I noticed that I began using online shopping much more often. 
    My headline would be "How did COVID leave a lasting impact?"

raw_comment:
What do you notice: 
    I notice that some graphs show that covid has made a lasting impact on our lives today. For example, there has been an increase in things like used car parts and online shopping since the pandemic, as well as a decrease in time socializing with others and test scores. This data shows how Covid has influenced how we live our lives today.
    
    What do you wonder:
    I wonder if there are parts of our lives that have not changed due to the pandemic. Are there graphs that would show a steady trend? What categories would these graphs be in? (Social, economic, education, labor)
    
    How does this relate to you and your community:
    This relates to me and my community because almost all of us were impacted heavily by the pandemic. I notice these things in my day-to-day life, for example, technology is now used a lot more for communication. Things like texting, social media, and calling are more normalized than they were before the pandemic.
    
    Catchy headline:
    “The lasting effects of Covid-19”

Something that I notice from the graphs is that you can clearly see when the new variants of Covid were introduced, as there are steep peaks every few months or so under the Total US Deaths graph.
    I wonder why the graph shows that the money spent on restaurants has now surpassed what the public spends on groceries. Is it because we are trying to compensate/ counteract for the time what we had lost so we are now overspending on social experiences?

I was not able to connect or communicate with my friends and family as much as others unfortunately.
    And finally as for the catchy title, I propose: Covid’s Causes Consequential ‘Conomy Crashes

raw_comment:
I noticed that the economy got a lot worse. The demand for jobs probably went up a lot because there were a lot less of them due to businesses having to cut costs, and some people who hadn't been working had to enter the workforce in order to support themselves and their families. 
    
    I wonder how this short period of bad economics, low test scores, and alternative ways of doing things is going to affect us long term. I want to know how some of the new things that were invented or popularized during the pandemic are going to continue to play a role in our society after the pandemic has mostly gone away. 
    
    The pandemic has affected me and my community by introducing new systems and technology. I think the damage to the economy and loss of life will blow over in the long term but the things we did to slow the pandemic and keep our lives as normal as we could will stick around. We don't always get snow days anymore, and when people are sick they sometimes wear masks even if they don't have COVID 19. 
    
    "Pandemic Pandemonium; How The Pandemic Caused Chaos"

I noticed that almost every graph had a major shift during Covid-19. This shows the extent to which the pandemic impacted day to day life. raw_comment:
I noticed the graphs collectively illustrate significant changes in key indicators during the pandemic era, particularly with spikes and drops in total deaths and unemployment rates in the United States. 
    
    I wondered how the trends in total deaths compare with those in unemployment. Is there a visible gap between public health impacts and economic effects?
    
    This relates to my community because, when we had quarantine and had to do online school, I remember playing a lot more video games as a way to socialize. I also remember that most resteraunts were close or only doordash so we never went out and only ordered food. I remember I was lucky enough to never get covid; a lot of people around me had it including my whole family. 
    
    How the pandemic changed our lives, from what the numbers tell us.

raw_comment:
I noticed that most of the graphs displayed a trend that was predictable, or showed the result that you would probably expect, which, in some cases, is concerning or sad, but in others is reassuring that everyone was having similar experiences.
    I wonder about why some of them differ somewhat from how you might expect them to look. For example, the reading and math levels for 3rd graders was a lot less extreme than i would expect, seeing as the biggest dip only went to about half a year behind - still not good, but not as far as I'd have thought.
    This relates to my community because, when we had to quarantine and do school online, I went into my neighbor's basement every day with a couple other kids and we all did it together. This made it more fun/tolerable, and I think I probably did better in school because of it. I wonder if other people had similar experiences, and if maybe that's why the reading and math levels graph wasn't as extreme as I expected.
    I would title these graphs "Statistics from the Social Distance"

## 1. Chart type
A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |
raw_comment: I noticed that activities like socializing and spending money on food/restaurants decreased, while things like self hair cutting and online shopping increased, showing how the pandemic made people rely more on themselves and the internet rather than other people. I wonder why deaths increase towards the end/start of each year, and why scores went down during the pandemic instead of up. This relates to me and my community because we all grew up and experienced this together. I remember driving by peoples houses for birthdays, online learning, and getting on video games and zoom calls with my friends. It really was a pivotal moment in my life and even though it was scary and frustrating, there were many times I wish I could go back and enjoy them again. My title for these nine graphs is "The Effect of COVID-19: How the Pandemic Reshaped American Life"

raw_comment:
I notice that all of these statistics were affected super harshly by the pandemic. I notice that a lot more women are working than pre-pandemic. I notice that “Unemployment claims” and “‘How to cut your own hair’” graphs are nearly identical.
        I wonder how many people were put out of a job because of the pandemic. Unemployment claims skyrocketed, restaurants, small businesses, anything that wasn’t a corporate giant closed due to the lack of consumers out and about. Would that graph look similar? How did they get the “time spent socializing with others” stats? What’s with the spike pattern on the “Deaths” graph?
        I remember a lot of my favorite mom-and-pop shops closing in 2020. My favorite restaurant that was next to my old house, Harriet’s, wasn’t able to stay open very long. I’ve watched the decline in reading and math comprehension in my little siblings/cousins, and I look at the climbing used car prices and wonder if I’ll really have to save that much.
        “The scale of COVID-19”

A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |

What do you notice:
    The big thing that I have noticed is how drastically things change once covid hits, and often in a way that is terrible for the community. For example, prices start going up, unemployment start going up, and so does deaths. 
     
    What do you wonder:
    I wonder if there are any graphs that were changed for the better at all. All of these are graphs that are showing negative or neutral shifts, but I am curious if covid's hit had any benefits to the community at all. 
    
    How does this relate to my community:
    This relates to our community because when we were all growing up together, we did a lot of it online. I remember doing homework over call with my friends and having socially distanced birthday parties. However, I also remember spending a lot more time with my family, and a lot more time outside. This is probably because family is who you quarantined with and being outside made things
    
    Catchy Headline:
    How covid drastically changed our lives forever.
