raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I notice that right when covid hits all the graphs take an unexpected turn. For example, how to cut your own hair searches increased by a lot. I also noticed that there were graphs that took a big dip like time socialising with others. during covid we were stuck in our houses and couldn't socialise with others as much
    What do you wonder?
        I wonder if there are any unexpected graphs that did not change. For example maybe there are           graphs that stayed relatively the same when covid hit. Maybe it could be something like the average amount of money spent at the grocery store or gas used in the average car. 
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to my community because me and my friends got hit by covid pretty hard. There are graphs about average test scores for kids and I am wondering if I contribute to that.
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea?
    We all know covid-19 affected us all, but I bet you didn’t expect how much it affected random things found in these graphs.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed a distinctive pattern in the total US deaths per week. The deaths are at their lowest around the middle of the summer and at their highest around winter and the holidays. I assume this is due to colder weather, more drinking, more stress, and being inside much more.
    2. Used car prices shot up at the start of the pandemic, peaking in early 2022. My understanding is that this was due to factors such as supply chains shutting down, putting increased demand on the used car market.
    3. Test scores for reading had already been going way down since 2017, and stayed on the same path through the pandemic until 2022. Math scores only started dropping in 2019, however. I wonder if this has less to do with the pandemic as it does with other factors?

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
    The graphs shown display trends before and after the pandemic took place. For example, we see unemployment claims rise dramatically after March 2020. The graphs paint a picture of a declining society, with a concerning statistic about reading and math levels in 3th - 8th graders being behind 0.2 - 0.4 years behind at most recent (2023). Luckily, those seem to be on the rise, and it will be very interesting to see if math and reading levels will be restored to at least the 2019 baseline in the future. 
    
    2) What do you wonder?
    I wonder why the share of women in the labor force went down during the pandemic, but then went back up following 2021. Were women disproportionately affected when job layoffs occurred during the pandemic?
    
    3) How does this relate to you and your community?
    To put it plainly, I had to live through the pandemic. I got to see these changes in real time, hearing about unemployment, having to do online shopping myself, watching used car prices spike.
    
    4) Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    Post-Pandemic Trends: How Are We Recovering?

raw_comment:
I'm noticing big spikes around March of 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, but I am also noticing that the trends are almost, if not already at what their previous trends were pre pandemic. This looks like on average it was happening in the middle of 2022. I am also noticing that restaurant prices are still higher than money spent on groceries, as well as that despite the pandemic minimizing the amount of women in the work force for a period of time, that number is still increasing significantly. 
    
    I wonder about the trends that have been changed and have not returned to what they once were. For example, the restaurant prices as opposed to the grocery prices, as well as the US test scores being at a significant low for some time now. How long do people think it will be before US test scores return to what the 2019 baseline is? When looking at the graph representing time socializing with others, I am wondering what the units were that were being used for this. Was it on a daily, weekly, or monthly basis that they were being tracked? 
    
    In connection with my community, many small businesses that closed can be seen when driving through Minneapolis. Additionally, online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic was the thing that I experienced first hand because so many students felt that they were behind for missing so much in person school to partake in social distancing. I would call this graph, "Adjustment to Life After a Pandemic."

raw_comment:
I notice that COVID had a big national impact on the world, but then had a lasting impact, with some being good and some being poor. The grades going down and socialization going down sadden me the most because people need communication to stay happy. This also shows that COVID had people being less engaged and more distracted, which is what the grades show. It is good, though, that restaurants are making a comeback from the big decline from the initial COVID-19 hit.
    
    I noticed some spikes and falls that were either before and after COVID-19 and I wonder what those could be from. The new deaths could've been the new varients of COVID. Socializing was also going down from before COVID. what could those be from?
    
    I have seen firsthand the fall in grades and people taking it less seriously, but I have also seen more women leaving jobs to take care of kids, and them getting put in hard positions from that. I know someone who lost their job presently, but it was still from the downsizing that COVID started initially. That just proves the point that this has a long-lasting effect.
    
    "COVID is hitting the world in many ways."

raw_comment:
I noticed the fact that spending on groceries rose while restaurant spending was consistently shifting. This can be attributed to the rising grocery costs and inflation effects on the economy. This is also seen in the used car costs where they raised ~40% from 2018.
    
    I wonder how the stay at home orders were able to cause such great shifts in the trends from the supply chain issues to the demand shifts of a non commuting society.
    
      I live in a small community in Massachusetts that is a tourist destination. Due to our community being fully reliant upon the people who come during the summer season, nearly all businesses had to downsize; both big and small. This led to greater unemployment and increased e-commerce as there were no longer any small local businesses around to support.
    
    "Pandemic's waves"

1. What do I notice?
    I notice that there is an obvious spike or decrease in the data on all the graphs once it hits march 2020. It so happens this is when COVID hit and quarantine became a thing. This can be seen through the  U.S. total deaths, unemployment rates, online shopping, and many more charts showing how COVID affected this data. When COVID hit, our world changed dramatically because it was a deadly virus that people didn't know how to cure. This is why it had such an effect on peoples lives and health.

    I wonder why the graph showing the amount of socializing every day only dropped 6 minutes. I thought it would be so much more.

    This relates to me because personally I have experienced many of the things that happened on these graphs. When COVID hit, our family started buying groceries and storing them in our freezer downstairs. We also started online shopping much more. Everything changed in a matter of a couple of days. 
    4. Create a catchy headline that captures the graphs main idea
    "How does one virus change billions of lives?"

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
    I notice that the COVID-19 pandemic caused major shifts in nearly every part of American life. Deaths, unemployment rates, and web searches like “how to cut your own hair” increased around March 2020. Spending habits changed (more groceries, fewer restaurants), online shopping, and car prices skyrocketed. Student learning fell behind — especially in math.
    
    What do I wonder? 
    I wonder if things will ever go back to how they were before COVID. 
    
    How does this relate to you and your community? 
    This relates to me and my community because we felt many of these effects.
    
    Catchy headline: 
    Life Before, During, and After 2020: How big of a change?

raw_comment:
When looking at the nine graphs regarding changes in Americans lives due to the Covid-19 pandemic, I noticed that at the time time covid hit, all of the data points saw SIGNIFICANT increases or decreases. A few of the data points had a trend pre-covid of seeing significant increases and decreases, so this wasn't completely out of the ordinary, but some, such as unemployment claims, saw completely uncharacteristic changes. 
    I wonder why costs of items such as used cars and food have not returned to the "normal" prices from before the pandemic?
    This information relates to me and my community because things such as cost of food, test scores, death totals and time spent socializing with others have impacts on the people around me. They effect community members mental health and quality of life. Spending less time around others weakens community bonds, unemployment causes economic struggles, and deaths hurt people and families in every way.
    A catchy headline for these graphs is "Covid Causes Change"

raw_comment:
I notice an increase in things like U.S deaths, women in the labor force, used car prices, online shopping.  With other things seeing a dramatic increase or decrease during the initial lockdown, such as unemployment claims, money spent on restaurants.  Some things which saw a decrease after the pandemic are reading and math scores from 3rd grade through 8th, as well as time spent socializing. 
    
    
    I wonder if our political leaders and government are trying to fix and revert the damages caused by the pandemic, and if so, how. I also wonder why there has been an increase in women in the labor force that is higher than even prior to the pandemic.  I also wonder why used car prices have increased so dramatically and exponentially after the pandemic.
    
    
    These graphs relate to me and my community as they are averages among the entire U.S, which would include me and my community.  Additionally, these graphs accurately describe the trends seen to this day, with lower time spent socializing and poorer exam scores among the youth.  All which I can attest to.
    
    
    “America: an uncertain future”

raw_comment:
When looking at the nine graphs, it’s really interesting to see the trend in each graph post-pandemic. Some of the trends returned to “normal” (pre-pandemic), while others show patterns different than they were pre-pandemic.  
    
    While most of the patterns after the pandemic make sense, the one I wonder about is the graph about money spent on food. I wonder what the reason is for why people are typically spending more money at restaurants than they are on groceries following the pandemic when prior to the pandemic they were not. 
    
    All of the information from these graphs reflects how life has changed for me and my community as a result of the pandemic. The graph that stands out to me the most from a personal standpoint is the huge spike in used car prices. As a future educator, the graph comparing reading and math scores is particularly disheartening as it’s now a goal of educators to catch up to the past data. Most scary is the fact that while the death rate continues to fluctuate in a similar pattern as pre-pandemic, overall more people are dying than before the pandemic. 
    
    Catchy Headline: What’s New in the “New Normal” World?

A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |

raw_comment:
When looking at these graphs, it’s clear how much the COVID-19 pandemic affected our daily lives and the lives of others. From socializing to education to employment, the pandemic had an immediate and sweeping effect. US students in grades 3–8 saw test scores plummet in both math and reading, probably because of so many people switching to online learning.
    
    Additionally, millions more people almost immediately lost their jobs and claimed unemployment, and people started eating out much less often. I wonder what kind of effect that had on the American economy with so much less money circulating suddenly. I also wonder if the online shopping market would have risen so sharply if there had not been a pandemic, as our shopping has become increasingly digital even without the pandemic, and it looks like the trend was going upwards anyway. Finally, I wonder why some of the spikes in the graphs happen a decent time after COVID-19 hit and why the effects were delayed in some areas.
    
    This closely relates to me and my country because I had to attend school online in 2020 and personally experienced the global wave of social isolation the pandemic caused. Looking back on it, it’s crazy to see the impact on all aspects of life, and it truly shows how much our lives were reshaped.
    
    I would call these graphs “How Covid-19 reshaped our lives overnight.”

A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.

1) In most, if not all of the graphs, the results after the pandemic are very concerning. While many expressed negative results, some graphs returned to normal. It was obvious that the greatest impacts of Covid were the deaths and damaged social infrastructure. Scores for education immediately spiked down along with socializing with others. The pandemic created an environment that made society more comfortable with technology than directly interacting with another. Prices also changed drastically as supply and demand continuously varied.
    2) Why do some issues plateau but others continue to spike after the pandemic? As we only focusing on certain issues or is this just naturally occurring?
    3) These results prove to be true in the patterns of my community. Many negative effects have occurred such as higher prices, reduced scores, and reduced social ability. However, since we have recovered from the pandemic, I have noticed social ability start to re-rise.
    4) The Pungent Products of the Pandemic

1. What do you notice?
    I notice that after the pandemic, fewer people socialize with one another. I also noticed an increase in the number of deaths after the pandemic. Online shopping has increased over the last five years. Many students, after the pandemic, have decreased their interest in learning, and now many students are falling behind.
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    I wonder if the reason behind students falling behind as to going remote for almost 2 years to going back to normal school? How come the increase of used cars has increased after the pandemic? 
    
    3. How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to me and my community because many of us shop online for most of our things. Many kids struggled with the idea of going back to school after doing remote learning for almost 2 years.
    
    4. Catchy Headline 
    “Life in the Time of COVID: The Transformative Impact on American Daily Life!”

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    
    I notice that as the COVID-19 pandemic hit, originally a lot of the graphs had sharp negative spikes due too the effects of being unable to live a traditionally life during that time period. However, a  lot of the graphs later returned to their original trends as people's lifestyles returned to normal societal progression continued.
    
    What do you wonder?
    
    One main thing that I wonder is why the reading trend started to bounce back after COVID even though it wasnt affected by the pandemic originally and their original trajectory mostly just continued. I also wonder why the time socializing with others is recovering so slowly after the COVID-19 pandemic, as I would have predicted that it would have spiked upward much higher than it actually did.
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    
    It personally affects me and my community locally, as well as the entire world in a variety of ways. The pandemic has set new trends in used car prices and in online shopping that has yet to recover. The used car prices hurts people trying to buy cars in my community and the online shopping trends hurt small businesses in my community. Also, the reading and math decreases will permanently harm the future because that generation of children will be slightly less proficient in the workforce.
    
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    
    COVID-19: The Downward Spiral

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
    A clear theme emerges across these graphs: although the pandemic occurred five years ago, its impact continues to linger. Academic performance has yet to fully recover, vehicle prices remain elevated, and most significantly, our levels of social interaction are still noticeably lower than before. There is no clear indication of when, or if, these trends will return to pre-pandemic norms.
    2) What do you wonder?
    What will society look like in twenty or thirty years? Will the decline in standardized testing outcomes lead to shortages in certain professions? Could this hinder technological and scientific progress? I also wonder are the unseen, lasting effects on our ability to connect with one another with us being disconnected for so long?
    3) How does this relate to you and your community?
    Perhaps the most vital part of our lives is human connection. One might assume that, once the world reopened, our social behaviors would bounce back to normal. Yet the data and my personal experience tells a different story. Sometimes, classrooms seem quieter, and students interact and participate less than they did before. It’s unnerving to think that the pandemic may have permanently reshaped how we interact with each other.
    4) What’s going on in this graph?
    A Silent Aftermath: How COVID-19 Changed the Way We Learn, Spend, and Connect

raw_comment: From these graphs I noticed  that a lot of the graphs either spike or make a dramatic drop in the year 2020 during Covid-19. One thing that I wonder from the graphs in the article is that after covid, people started going out to restaurants more often because they missed the feeling of being able to dine out but then why didn't this same feeling of missing out apply to socializing after covid? As the graphs show, the amount of socializing during pre-covid was much higher than post-covid. This relates to me and my community because I and other people I have talked to about the ability to socialize after covid have felt that they are less social than they were before and felt a loss of social skills and maturity. I think another headline that this article could have to sum up the main idea would be, “How Did Covid-19 Impact Americans Everyday Lives?”

raw_comment: The pandemic has affected every aspect of American's lives. Deaths, Unemployment claims, Money spent on food, car prices, online shopping, and share of women in labor force all increased. On the other hand test scores as well as time socializing with others greatly decreased. All this is very alarming to me and demonstrates a dramatic change in the average American's lives. I wonder if the graphs will ever return to how they were before the pandemic.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    
    I notice a common theme between these graphs: while the pandemic occurred five years ago, its consequences and lasting effects remain apparent. Test scores remain down, car prices remain up, and most importantly our time socializing with others is still considerably low. There is no certainty when these graphs will return to their norms. 
    
    What do you wonder?
    
    I wonder what the lasting effect of this pandemic will be. Test scores are worrisome because they gain a gist of the general intelligence of the future. How will our society look in several decades? Will these stem-related jobs be filled, or will the decrease in standardized testing prove fatal, resulting in gaps throughout our most innovative jobs? These questions are unknown, but the question that particularly worries me is about the social impact. What is the cost of human isolation for several years?
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    
    Arguably the most imperative aspect of our lives is how we interact with others. When you pause this interaction for two years many would assume it would go right back up to its normal state. However since the graph shows that is not the case, we know this isolation has lasting effects. Even in my school classes remain quieter than they used to be before the pandemic. It is truly a complete unknown as to how this pandemic will affect us in the years to come.

raw_comment:
Due to COVID-19, the US was faced with many new economic changes, many of which were detrimental problems. The graphs illustrate a negative rate of change in unemployment; however, a positive rate of change in the online business industry. Unfortunately, the majority of these graphs report an extremely detrimental series of events resulting from the pandemic, such as death and the unemployment rate.

I wonder why deaths go up and down every couple years. raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
    I noticed how all of these graphs had a large spike around March 2020. We can see higher death rates, more unemployment, and dropping scores. Some of these graphs were able to get back to their normal trends, but others weren't able to recover.
    2) What do you wonder?
    I wonder why the death rates are still higher than they were from 2015-2019. I also wonder if the used car prices will go back down because they are still much higher than they were pre-pandemic.
    3) How does this relate to you and your community? 
    This relates to me because I remember going through all of this from 5th-6th grade and remember how it affected me.
    4) Pandemic Panic: How the World Changed...

raw_comment:
I am devastated to see the dramatic amount of deaths going on during Covid-19, this chart reveals how many people die in the U.S. each week. But it skyrockets when the pandemic occurs, it shows the effect of what the disease has done to our society and its everlasting effects. 
    In the second graph, we can observe that the pandemic has turned many innocent people's lives around, we can see the escalation of unemployment claims due to many businesses shutting down. I am very sorrowful for those who had to go through this, yet I am satisfied enough to see that millions of people have bounced back and got jobs within a year.
    Transitioning on to the third, I am baffled and unaware until now about how many women are in our labor force as of today. I notice a positive trend showing how it is going to continue to keep going up. It makes me ponder how women got here in the first place.
    On the fourth, I can extremely relate, I like to spend lots of money on food, but have never noticed how much each individual spends in comparison to groceries and restaurants. 
    With the fifth, we can notice an increased price in used cars due to the supply chain disruptions during the pandemic.
    I can take part to the sixth, as almost everyone had to shop online because during the pandemic, no one could go outside.
    Many people could interact with eachother during covid so they had to chat online
    Many people didn't try during school in the pandemic, I personally only had 3 hours of school in 2020
    8 cool

## 1. Chart type
A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |

raw_comment:
When looking at these graphs I see multiple spikes during the Pandemic era. This is shown in the spike of unemployment claims in 2020, and the loss of time socializing with others. I wonder why the deaths in the US had so many up and down spikes, which is still seen today, although less extreme. These graphs relate to me and my community because the graphs and their spikes were definitely present in my community, a drop in socializing with others and in increase in staying inside and buying groceries instead of going out to eat. 
    A headline for this could be- Covid 19: The Up and Down spikes caused by the coronavirus that affected our lives back in 2020 and still affect our lives 5 years later.

## 1. Chart type
A **grid of small-multiple time-series line charts**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting**: 9 separate panels, each showing a different topic.
- **Shared temporal layout**: all panels use time on the x-axis.
- **Color segmentation by period**: pre–March 2020 values are shown in gray/black; post–March 2020 values in orange.
- **Multiple lines within some panels**: e.g., food spending and test scores compare two categories in the same panel.
- **Reference lines / annotations**: dashed or solid baseline/trend lines and text labels appear in some panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (2015–2024, with March 2020 marked) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Panel topic / metric (e.g., Total U.S. deaths, Unemployment claims, Online shopping, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Total U.S. deaths per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| 2015–19 average (deaths) | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; label |
| Unemployment claims per week | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Share of women in the labor force | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Subgroup: women 25 to 54 who have a child under 5 | Categorical/nominal | Subtitle/label defining the series |
| Money spent on food | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; panel metric/title |
| Food spending category: Restaurants | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Food spending category: Groceries | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Monthly spending amount ($ billions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line values |
| Used car prices (increase from 2016 prices) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Feb. 2022 | Temporal | Annotation label marking a point in time |
| Online shopping share of retail sales | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Prepandemic trend | Quantitative | Dashed reference/trend line; label |
| Time socializing with others (minutes) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| U.S. scores, 3rd grade through 8th | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; lines |
| Subject: Reading | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| Subject: Math | Categorical/nominal | Separate line; direct label/color |
| 2019 baseline | Quantitative | Horizontal reference line; label |
| Performance relative to grade level / years ahead-behind | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| “How to cut your own hair” web searches | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; line |
| Search interest (% of peak interest) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Period relative to March 2020 (pre/post) | Temporal / ordinal | Line color (gray before, orange after); background shading transition |

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
    
    I notice that each of the graphs show quality of life after after COVID. I notice in all graphs spiked following COVID, and only some of them returned to normal following the "end" of COVID.
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    
    I suppose I wonder why some of the problems created by COVID are still so very ongoing. For example why do some increased pricing ranges not go down, while others do.
    
    3. How does this relate to me and my community?
    
    This will always relate to me and my community because we have all been affected by COVID 19 in so many ways. Fortunately, no one in my family passed away because of COVID. Despite this, COVID has still had a lasting effect on all of us. Many of these statistics are shocking at first, but the more I see them, the more this all makes sense. I guess it's eye opening to see the true scale of some of the damage COVID caused.
    
    4. What is going on in this graph?
    
    This graph is demonstrating the effects of COVID 19, on 9 separate statistics.

raw_comment:
1) These graphs focus on trends of changes in behavior spending habits before during and after COVID-19. There are massive shifts in spending on food, socializing, car prices, online shopping and interest. There is also a decline in the academic performances from 3rd-8th grade. 
    2) I wonder how long lasting these changes are? will all these trends revert to pre COVID? or will they stay permanent 
    3) As a High school senior, COVID started when I wee little lad in 7th grade. The graph that I can relate the most with is the one about cutting hair. My sister would cut my hair for me. She ended up using the wrong type of blade so it not only hurt but it wasn't my sharpest hair cut, But it was better than nothing. 
    4) My title would be "Pandemic's Ripple Effect: How COVID-19 Reshaped Our Lives."

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
    Within these graphs, the first thing that I notice is that after the year 2020, every graph has a substantial difference. Whether it be a huge drop, or a huge rise, every graph has a change. 
    2) What do you wonder?
    The initial thing I wondered while looking at these graphs was "how did they get this information?" I am wondering if they sent surveys out, what resources they looked at to get the numbers, and how they picked the people? I also wondered how they decided to make these prompts the data that they looked at out of all of the things that could have been influenced by the pandemic.
    3) How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to me and my community because being from a small town, something like this can have a huge impact. When one person gets sick, a big percent of people get sick since there aren't many people and we are seeing the same people over and over. It also was difficult for people in my community to completely quarantine because most people were essential workers. 
    4) Aftermath of Covid: How the Pandemic Affects Us

    4)“Masks Off, Minds Blown: Life After the Lockdown”

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
    I noticed a drastic change in March of 2020 when the pandemic occurred in these graphs. Afterward, some of the graphs gradually found their way back to the trend it was originally following. However, for some of the graphs (U.S. Scores, Time socializing with others, and Used car prices), the data post-pandemic is vastly different than the pre-pandemic trend. 
    
    2) What do you wonder?
    I wonder why certain things, like Used car prices, are so different after the pandemic. Some graphs make sense, for example, such as Time socializing with others where we were not able to socialize during quarantine, proceeded to get used to the lifestyle, then were able to become social again but we had already acclimated to being more anti-social. 
    
    3) How does this relate to you and your community?
    As a now-college student, I was in high school during the pandemic. During quarantine, I remember when all of my classes became pass-fail, and the motivation to work hard at my classes was diminished. I feel like my peers in college would agree that it was difficult to get "back in the swing of things" once quarantine was over in terms of academics and social skills. This graph reflects that. 
    
    4) Create a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
    
    Pre to Post-Pandemic: What's the Difference?

raw_comment:
1)The charts indicate how life in America significantly changed due to the COVID-19 pandemic and how some of its effects remained until 2024. Death rates skyrocketed much greater than prior to the pandemic, and unemployment claims temporarily peaked before stabilizing again. People redirected expenditure from dining out to food shops, and online shopping accelerated at an even greater rate than prior to it. Student scores on tests, especially in math, fell and are still partially recovering, and social interaction is still below prior levels. Several trends, for example, greater labor force participation of women with young children, show lasting positive change, while others reflect ongoing challenge in a return to pre-pandemic status.
    2)Looking at these charts, I wonder which of these pandemic-driven changes will become permanent parts of society and which will eventually revert. For example, will the shift toward online shopping and increased grocery spending continue growing, or plateau?
    3)For me, living in New Jersey, a lot of what’s shown in these charts really hits home. I remember how intense those early months of the pandemic were—so many people around me got sick or lost someone, and the spike in deaths felt very real
    4)“From Lockdown to Lookin’ Up: Life After the Masked Era”

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
    I noticed that during March 2020 no matter what the graph was about all of them had some sort of spike. Solitary activities like online shopping, 'How to cut your own hair' web searches, and unemployment claims increased juristically. While typical group activities like money spent on restaurants, U.S. education scores, and time socially with others had a major decrease. 
    
    2) What do you wonder?
    I wonder why the time socializing with others had a large fall around 2019 before the pandemic started, when most other graphs had their major peaks close to around when the pandemic started in March 2020?
    
    3) How does this relate to you and your community?
    In my community I have seen firsthand in classrooms how the averages of test scores for younger kids has significantly gone down since the pandemic, which is also evident in the graph. 
    
    4) Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    'How COVID 19 changed our habits'

raw_comment:
I noticed that in everyone of these graphs when Covid-19 occurred something drastic happened in either increasing or decreasing in numbers. For example unemployment claims skyrocketed in March 2020 when Covid was in full fledged lockdown. The same thing with searches of “How to cut your own hair?” occurred. 
        I wonder why the used car prices reached their peak in February 2022 specifically? Is it a result of the pandemic,but why?
        I can relate one of the graphs to my own community because many barber shops were closed, and my brother's hair was atrocious! So, he asked me to cut his hair and I knew I had to look up how to cut your own hair! I could say I was apart of that spike in searches. 
        A catchy title: COVID-19 and it’s impact.

raw_comment:
I noticed that there was a drastic decline in the "time socializing with others" from around 2019 to 2021. This rapid change is from the COVID-19 pandemic, causing people to quarantine, resulting in lack of personal interaction. 
    I wonder if the spike in online shopping will only increase from 2020 and future years to come? Obviously not being allowed in person to different stores/shops, there was an increase in online shopping, so with this new activity normalized and often used, will this affect the activity of in person shopping? Since we all got so used to online shopping, it might be hard for business to gain a steady income again for in person sales due to the consistency we all endured from the Pandemic.
    This connects to my community especially during times of COVID as we had to experience these changes from in person living lifestyles, but also from online and social media presence. Our society has been heavily altered from the dependency on social media because of the isolation we all had to do from quarantining. 
    "Life Post-Lock Down"

    Title
    Coronavirus Pandemic: A Twisted Turn on Life

raw_comment:
Looking across the graphs, it’s clear how deeply the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted daily life from education to employment. U.S. students in grades 3 through 8 experienced major drops in both reading and math scores, likely reflecting the challenges of remote learning.
    
     At the same time the labor force saw a sharp decline in women’s participation in March 202, I wonder whether the pandemic also played a role in the recent rebound of women rejoining the workforce.
    
    These shifts hit close to home not just from what we saw in our own communities, but also from what we experienced through social media: a global wave of isolation, adaptation, and change. Activities that relied on being in person, like school or salon visits, plummeted, while internet searches for DIY fixes like cutting your own hair exploded. It’s a strange, striking look at how much our lives were reshaped.
    
     "Life, Disrupted: A Pandemic Snapshot"
